facts.claim: Drought settled over the southern Plains and the Dust Bowl began
facts.context: The rains failed across Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas in 1930, and ploughed-up land that had once been grass started to blow away.
facts.goDeeper: The dust reached far beyond the farms it came from: storms in 1934 dropped Plains soil on Chicago, Washington and ships out in the Atlantic.

facts.claim: Troops drove the Bonus Army of jobless veterans out of their camp in Washington
facts.context: Thousands of unemployed First World War veterans camped in the capital asking for their service bonus early, and the Army cleared the camp in July 1932.
facts.goDeeper: The officers who carried out the eviction included Douglas MacArthur, Dwight Eisenhower and George Patton, all three of whom would command in the next war.

facts.claim: Franklin Roosevelt was elected president, turning Herbert Hoover out of office
facts.context: Roosevelt carried 42 of the 48 states in November 1932, though he did not take office until the following March.
facts.goDeeper: That four-month wait was the last of its kind: the Twentieth Amendment moved the inauguration to January so a stricken country never had to wait again.

facts.claim: Roosevelt closed every bank in the country for four days
facts.context: Two days after taking office in March 1933 he shut the banks nationwide, and only those inspected and judged sound were allowed to open again.
facts.goDeeper: It worked as much by nerve as by law: when the doors opened, people queued to put their money back in rather than to take it out.

facts.claim: Roosevelt spoke straight to the country by radio in the first fireside chat
facts.context: On 12 March 1933 he explained the banking crisis to people sitting in their own front rooms, the first of some thirty such broadcasts.
facts.goDeeper: He wrote them for the ear rather than the hall, in short common words, and opened by calling the audience his friends.

facts.claim: The worst dust storm of the Dust Bowl turned a Sunday afternoon black
facts.context: On 14 April 1935 a wall of dust rolled across the southern Plains and blotted out the sun in the middle of the day.
facts.goDeeper: A reporter who watched it coming wrote the phrase dust bowl in his copy the next day, and the name stuck to the whole region and the whole decade.

facts.claim: The Social Security Act created old-age pensions for American workers
facts.context: Signed in August 1935, it set up retirement payments funded by a tax on wages, alongside unemployment insurance.
facts.goDeeper: The first monthly cheque went out in 1940 to Ida May Fuller of Vermont for $22.54; she lived to 100 and collected for 35 years.

facts.claim: Hoover Dam was finished and handed over to the federal government
facts.context: The dam on the Colorado River was completed on 1 March 1936, more than two years ahead of its schedule.
facts.goDeeper: Around 21,000 men worked on it, many arriving in the desert with their families and nowhere at all to live, so a whole town was built to hold them.

facts.claim: Strikers sat inside General Motors plants in Flint until the company recognised their union
facts.context: Workers occupied the factories from the end of December 1936 and stayed inside for 44 days, until GM agreed in February 1937 to bargain with the United Auto Workers.
facts.goDeeper: Sitting down inside the plant rather than picketing outside it made replacement workers useless, and union membership across the country multiplied in the years that followed.

facts.claim: John Steinbeck published The Grapes of Wrath
facts.context: His novel about a tenant family driven off their land and heading west came out in April 1939 and was the best-selling book of the year.
facts.goDeeper: It was banned from libraries and burned in parts of California and Oklahoma for the picture it painted, and it won the Pulitzer Prize the year after.

facts.claim: Share of American workers with no job at the worst of the Depression
facts.context: Unemployment reached roughly a quarter of the workforce in 1933, and was still in double figures at the end of the decade.
facts.goDeeper: The figure counts only those actively looking for work, so it hides the millions more on short hours or scratching a living from odd jobs.

facts.claim: American banks that failed in the first years of the Depression
facts.context: Close to 9,000 banks went under between 1930 and 1933, and the people whose savings were inside them had no insurance to fall back on.
facts.goDeeper: That is what made a queue outside a bank so dangerous: a rumour could empty a perfectly sound one in a morning, because nobody wanted to be last in line.

facts.claim: Young men who worked in the Civilian Conservation Corps
facts.context: About three million passed through the camps between 1933 and 1942, planting trees, fighting fires and building the trails and shelters in the parks.
facts.goDeeper: The pay was $30 a month and $25 of it went straight home to the man's family, which was as much the point of the scheme as the trees were.

facts.claim: The first federal minimum wage, set in 1938, for an hour's work
facts.context: The Fair Labor Standards Act put a floor of 25 cents an hour under most wages, rising to 40 cents over the following seven years.
facts.goDeeper: The same law capped the ordinary working week at 44 hours and set a minimum age for most jobs, ending legal child labour across a great many trades.

facts.claim: The 1929 crash set off a wave of suicides among ruined Wall Street traders
facts.context: The image of brokers jumping from windows is largely legend: the suicide rate in New York rose only slightly, and there was no epidemic of leaps from Wall Street buildings.
facts.goDeeper: Newspapers printed the rumours as fact within days, and the picture stuck so hard that it now stands in for the whole crash.

facts.claim: Prohibition stayed the law of the land through the whole of the 1930s
facts.context: It was repealed in December 1933, less than a year into Roosevelt's first term, so most of the decade was legally wet.
facts.goDeeper: Hard times made the case: breweries and distilleries meant jobs and wages at a moment when almost nothing else was hiring.

facts.claim: The New Deal ended the Depression
facts.context: Unemployment fell a long way from its 1933 peak but stayed in double figures for the rest of the decade, and the economy only came fully back with war production in the 1940s.
facts.goDeeper: Economists still argue about how much the New Deal helped; almost none of them argue that it finished the job.

facts.claim: The Dust Bowl was made far worse by the way the Plains had been farmed
facts.context: High wheat prices and new tractors had turned over millions of acres of deep-rooted prairie grass, so when the drought came there was nothing left holding the soil down.
facts.goDeeper: One government answer was a shelterbelt of more than 200 million trees planted from Texas up to the Canadian border, to slow the wind across open fields.

facts.claim: Savings in a bank account were insured by the government for the first time in the 1930s
facts.context: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation was created in 1933, and once ordinary accounts were covered the era of mass bank runs was over.
facts.goDeeper: Roosevelt was doubtful about the idea and it came out of Congress rather than the White House, yet it outlasted almost everything else in the New Deal.

facts.claim: The economy fell back into a sharp slump in 1937 after years of recovery
facts.context: Output and jobs dropped steeply through 1937 and 1938, after federal spending was cut back and taxes rose, undoing a good deal of the recovery.
facts.goDeeper: People at the time called it the Roosevelt recession, and it is a large part of why the Depression is remembered as lasting a whole decade.
